subject: physics
title: Speed, velocity and distance–time graphs
key_idea: Speed is how fast something moves and has no direction. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Average speed is distance divided by time. The gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed.

blocks.text: This section covers four quantities that describe motion and which of them have a direction.

items.meaning: How far an object moves. It has no direction, so it is a scalar.
The distance in a straight line from the start to the finish, with its direction. It is a vector.
How fast an object moves. It has no direction, so it is a scalar.
The speed of an object in a given direction. It is a vector.

items: Two cars can have the same speed but different velocities if they move in different directions.
If the road bends, the direction changes, so the velocity changes.
The speed of a moving object is rarely constant, so we often use the average speed.
Distance and speed are scalars. Displacement and velocity are vectors.
Velocity is speed in a given direction.

blocks.text: This section covers how to measure the speed of an object such as a trolley, a toy car or a ripple.

items.text: Use a metre rule or marks a set distance apart.
Start a stopwatch at the first mark and stop it at the second. Or use a light gate to record the time.
Divide the distance by the time.
Repeat the measurement and calculate an average.

items: A light gate uses a beam of light and records the time it is interrupted.
To find the speed at the bottom of a slope, measure over a short distance at the bottom.
Timing the whole slope gives the average speed down the slope, not the speed at the bottom.
Record readings to a consistent number of decimal places.
Measure a distance and a time, then divide the distance by the time.
Repeat and average to improve the result.

blocks.text: This section covers how to read speed from a distance–time graph.

rows: The distance does not change, so the object is stationary.

items: The speed of an object is the gradient of its distance–time graph.
To find the gradient, divide the change in distance by the change in time.
Read the distance and time from the axes and keep the units in metres and seconds.
(AQA: Higher tier) For a curve, the speed at a time is the gradient of a tangent drawn at that time.
Speed is the gradient of a distance–time graph.
A horizontal line means stationary. A steeper line means a faster speed.

checks.q: The winner of a marathon runs 42 000 m in 5600 s. Calculate the average speed.
State the difference between speed and velocity.
checks.a: Speed has magnitude only and is a scalar. Velocity is speed in a given direction and is a vector.

checks.q: Describe how you could find the average speed of a ball bearing falling through a liquid.
checks.a: Measure a distance with a ruler and the time to fall that distance with a stop clock. Use speed = distance ÷ time. Repeat and average.

worked_example.question: A conveyor belt moves a can at a speed of 1.7 m/s. Calculate the time taken to move the can 3.3 m at this speed. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
worked_example.tip: The last mark is for rounding to 2 significant figures. A correctly rounded answer from a wrongly used value of the data can still score it.

items: Typical values are walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
The speed a person can walk, run or cycle depends on age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled.
(AQA: Higher tier) Motion in a circle has constant speed but changing velocity, because the direction keeps changing.

worked_example.question: A skier goes down a hill. Describe how her speed at the bottom of the slope could be determined.
answer_points: Measure a distance at the bottom, or use markers a certain distance apart.
Start a timer at the first marker.
Stop the timer at the second marker.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score. Using a light gate, not over the whole slope, is also accepted.

worked_example.question: A student drops a rock into a pond from a height of 1.5 m. The rock makes ripples. Describe how the student uses a metre ruler and a stop clock to determine the speed of the ripples.
answer_points: Use the metre ruler to measure a set distance the ripple travels.
Use the stop clock to measure the time for a ripple to travel the set distance.
worked_example.tip: Measuring the distance a ripple travels in a set time, or the time it takes to travel a set distance, scores 2 marks. There is a second method using wavelength × frequency.

worked_example.question:
A river flows at a speed of 0.54 m/s. A swimmer starts at point P and swims at a constant speed of 0.72 m/s relative to the water and at right angles to the current. After 1.5 minutes, the swimmer reaches point Q.

Calculate the distance between P and Q.
answer_points: The two speeds are at right angles, so the speed over the ground is √(0.54² + 0.72²) = 0.90 m/s.

extra.heading: Measuring small distances and short times

blocks.text: A single small distance or a short time is hard to measure accurately, so measure many of them together.

items: Time 20 swings of a pendulum and divide by 20 to find the period of one swing.
Measure the thickness of a stack of identical sheets and divide by the number of sheets.
Dividing by the number of repeats shares the timing error across all of them.
A horizontal line on a speed–time graph is a constant speed.
A line sloping up means the object is accelerating. A line sloping down means it is decelerating.
A line along the time axis, at zero speed, means the object is at rest.

worked_example.question:
An ultrasonic device sends a pulse of sound to a wall and receives the reflection. The sound travels at 345 m/s. The distance from the device to the wall is 2.35 m.

Calculate the time between the sound wave being emitted and received by the device.
answer_points: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the distance is doubled: 2 × 2.35 = 4.70 m
